title: AI in law (RollOnFriday discussion-board thread on training the next generation)
pub: RollOnFriday, main discussion board (anonymous UK lawyers' forum)
author: Anonymous RollOnFriday discussion-board participants

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The thread accepts the cluster’s core view that legal AI is uneven, task-specific and dependent on human supervision. It materially extends the synthesis with practitioner accounts of a key operating-model failure: firms seek complete complex outputs instead of decomposing work into suitable subtasks, while underinvestment in legal technology and information security obstructs adoption. Its evidence is primarily anecdotal rather than measured.
qs: This same issue haunts AI - unless it hands me back some perfect massively complex piece of work I can't be arsed, whereas there are literally thousands of "find and replace", get me halfway there etc.

The other problem in law is legal tech/infosec functions are largely shit because there is no investment in them and their brief is "don't fook up", not "get us ahead of those clowns across the road".

st.t: Associate training: Automation threatens expertise reproduction
st.an: The thread broadly supports the cluster’s core paradox: automating basic junior tasks may weaken experiential training while AI output still requires knowledgeable human verification. Its reported Copilot material also aligns with reconstructing training through simulation, AI-integrated curricula and deeper mentorship, though the discussion is anecdotal, speculative and not unified.
qs: If AI takes over basic tasks successfully, how will you train the newbies?
Their output needs to be reviewed and supervised by people who can actually recognise when those errors are made.

st.t: Law-firm pyramid: Efficiency threatens revenue and training
st.an: The thread supports the cluster’s central concerns by linking automation of basic junior tasks to a possible apprenticeship gap and by suggesting that firms could capture efficiency gains through fewer junior roles and higher partner income. It also echoes the need for expert human verification, but its evidence is anecdotal, speculative and internally disputed rather than demonstrative.
qs: If AI takes over basic tasks successfully, how will you train the newbies?

So no change really  Haven't seen any impact on profitability either for the worse or the better  But if we can get rid of say 50% of juniors on very big money, then it's more money for partners so it makes sense  ---  **[anonymous poster]**  So more law graduates contemplating suicide in their miserable tele-sales job then.

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: The thread supports the cluster’s central proposition: AI may absorb routine legal tasks and reduce junior work, but uneven output quality requires skilled human verification and creates a training-pipeline risk. Its claims are mainly anecdotal and predictive, and the adaptive-training proposals are attributed to Microsoft Copilot rather than clearly endorsed by participants.
qs: Their output needs to be reviewed and supervised by people who can actually recognise when those errors are made.
If AI takes over basic tasks successfully, how will you train the newbies?

st.t: Task substitution: Complementarity can still reshape staffing
st.an: The thread supports the cluster’s central proposition by depicting AI as capable of taking over bounded routine tasks while leaving strategy, supervision and judgment with lawyers, yet potentially changing junior staffing, training and the distribution of efficiency gains. Its conflicting anonymous anecdotes reinforce the cluster’s uncertainty about aggregate employment and profitability rather than establishing a single forecast.
qs: So no change really  Haven't seen any impact on profitability either for the worse or the better  But if we can get rid of say 50% of juniors on very big money, then it's more money for partners so it makes sense  ---  **[anonymous poster]**  So more law graduates contemplating suicide in their miserable tele-sales job then.

kp.k: Automation raises disputed questions about junior training and retention
kp.d: The opening post juxtaposes negative and conditional-positive assessments of AI output and asks how newcomers will learn if basic tasks are automated. It speculates that only big firms will continue taking juniors for succession and senior lawyers' status, potentially seeking 5+ year commitments or training-cost repayment. These are anonymous predictions, not reported employment changes.
qs: If AI takes over basic tasks successfully, how will you train the newbies?
AI produces great results if you use it properly
I'd expect big firms to try to tie juniors into 5+ year contracts or want some kind of training cost back

kp.k: Reported adoption has not yet changed profitability
kp.d: One participant reports extensive off-the-shelf and bespoke tools at their firm, used by younger staff, while partners continue concentrating on strategy, business development and management. They report no profitability impact so far, but suggest hypothetically that removing 50% of highly paid juniors would increase partner returns. No staffing reduction or supporting financial data is reported.
qs: Just like any big firm, we have lots of AI tools both off the shelf and bespoke
The young people do use them
The partners concentrate on strategic decisions, BD and management. So no change really
Haven't seen any impact on profitability either for the worse or the better
But if we can get rid of say 50% of juniors on very big money, then it's more money for partners so it makes sense

kp.k: Participants dispute comparative reliability but insist on supervision
kp.d: One participant argues that machine-learning errors require review by people capable of recognising them. Another predicts that AI will eventually make fewer errors than an exhausted transactional lawyer who has worked 70 of the last 100 hours. A separate participant also stresses supervision. The thread supplies neither measured error rates nor a demonstrated comparison.
qs: Even in a perfect world a % of error is inherent in all machine learning tools. Their output needs to be reviewed and supervised by people who can actually recognise when those errors are made.
ai over time will make far fewer errors that a deal gimp who's been in the office for 70 of the last 100 hours
it must however be supervised accordingly.

kp.k: Quoted Copilot response proposes redesigned legal apprenticeship
kp.d: A participant reproduces MS Copilot's answer rather than independently endorsing its proposals. The generated response predicts a shift from repetitive document review, contract analysis and research toward earlier strategy, negotiation and judgment, supported by simulations, technology-integrated curricula and deeper mentorship. It presents these as possible adaptations and maintains that ethical judgment and interpersonal skills remain human contributions.
qs: But that doesn’t mean the training pipeline disappears—it evolves.
With AI doing the rote work, trainees could focus sooner on higher-order thinking like litigation strategy, negotiation, or nuanced argumentation.
Law schools and firms might use advanced simulations or mock cases powered by AI to teach skills dynamically.
New lawyers could be trained not just in law, but in how to interpret and collaborate with AI tools.
Since mentors won’t be bogged down with basic tasks, they may invest more time guiding juniors through complex reasoning and client relations.

kp.k: Experience is asserted as a prerequisite for strategy
kp.d: A participant explicitly rejects the quoted AI answer's optimistic training account, arguing that strategic understanding depends on prior substantive experience. This directly contests the suggestion that juniors can simply move sooner into higher-order work when routine tasks disappear.
qs: That AI answer is utter bollocks. Unsurprisingly yet insidiously.
You can’t understand strategy unless and until you understand what you’re strategising. From experience.

kp.k: Prompting and model routing allegedly constrain useful outputs
kp.d: One participant claims that Copilot routes queries to models according to its own assessment and Microsoft's economy, potentially compromising results. They report finding no AI capable of dynamic document mark-ups despite examining multiple tools, speculate that this may change, and recommend investing time in prompting. These are participant claims and personal observations, not technical test results.
qs: The issue with MS Copilot is that, behind the scenes, it makes its own assessment of a query and then allocates the query to the AI model that itself deems fit (i.e. is most economical for MS).
That means that you may not get optimal results when asking MS Copilot.
I have looked at a whole range of AI over the years but so far, none have been able to offer dynamic mark-ups of documentation.
It is very much about learning to prompt right, and one should spend some time on that.

kp.k: Fragmented bespoke transaction materials allegedly limit legal AI
kp.d: A participant attributes difficulties to firm disorganisation, comparatively low transaction-document volumes and a lack of connections between bespoke precedents. Their illustrative estimate is that top European M&A firms generate 'maybe 1000 SPAs in a year'; it is not presented as study evidence. They argue that even a talented graduate could not readily turn that collection into a suitable transaction-specific agreement, contrasting this with repetitive NDAs.
qs: In my opinion legal AI struggles because law firms are so disorganised and the volume of material is comparatively low in transactional work e.g. the top M&A law firms in europe generate maybe 1000 SPAs in a year?
These are likely highly bespoke, and there is nothing to join the dots.
NDAs are the antithesis of this - they are largely a cut and paste joke that lawyers made money out of for far too long.

kp.k: Poor delegation obstructs both automation and trainee development
kp.d: Drawing an analogy with near-shoring, a participant argues that technologically enabled self-sufficiency and fear of career damage or litigation inhibit delegation. They also attribute inadequate training partly to selfishness and possibly reduced sociability following COVID. They contrast earlier discrete trainee assignments with current whole-deal allocation at their workplace, which favours experienced trainees, and argue that expecting perfect complex AI outputs overlooks numerous useful partial tasks.
qs: Many then have enormous difficulty letting go due to fear of career damage/litigation, so never e.g. break work down into manageable chunks suitable for delegation.
There is also a growth in selfishness and perhaps a COVID related lack of sociability that means people are not prepared to properly train and supervise.

This same issue haunts AI - unless it hands me back some perfect massively complex piece of work I can't be arsed, whereas there are literally thousands of "find and replace", get me halfway there etc. tasks that could be farmed out.
meaning 4th seaters are prized and 1st seaters are tolerated.

kp.k: Underinvestment and defensive mandates allegedly hinder legal technology
kp.d: A participant identifies legal-technology and information-security functions as an additional organisational obstacle, claiming that they lack investment and receive risk-avoidance rather than competitive-innovation mandates. This is an anonymous assessment rather than documented expenditure or performance evidence.
qs: The other problem in law is legal tech/infosec functions are largely shit because there is no investment in them and their brief is "don't fook up", not "get us ahead of those clowns across the road".

kp.k: Poor correspondence is attributed to AI without confirmation
kp.d: A participant reports receiving a very poor letter of claim bearing a partner's and senior associate's names and assumes it was AI-generated. The anecdote expresses concern about output quality but does not establish that AI produced the letter or identify any specific errors.
qs: I received a letter of claim recently which must have been produced by AI. No lawyer could possibly have written it ( though there was a partner and Snr Assoc named with it)
It was absolute shite.

kp.k: Standardisation offers a separate route to reducing routine work
kp.d: Participants discuss standard NDAs and data-processing agreements as ways to eliminate repetitive drafting, alongside a wish for AI to handle privacy work. This is a distinct standardisation argument, not evidence of AI capability. One participant argues that shared standards would free substantial time but expects that time to be filled with more work rather than a shorter working week.
qs: One area that would be great for AI to take over is data privacy. Data processing agreements etc.

There should just be a standard NDA and DPA that everyone uses. This would free up so much time (which would then need to be filled with other tasks because heaven forfend that we have a shorter working week).

kp.k: Distribution of productivity gains is a central concern
kp.d: One participant reframes the debate around how money is distributed rather than technical capability, asserting that universal 40+ hour working weeks have long been unnecessary. Together with concerns about graduate prospects and partner gains elsewhere in the thread, this identifies a distributional dispute, without supplying labour-market evidence or a concrete redistribution proposal.
qs: The real question is how the money gets distributed. It hasn’t been necessary for everyone to work 40+ hours a week for ages.

kp.k: AI filmmaking analogy exposes disagreement over comparison standards
kp.d: Participants debate an allegedly AI-only film made by a former ASML legal head in about a day. A defender values its speed and quality relative to ordinary corporate communications or amateur production; critics judge continuity and professional-film standards, question whether editing was automated, and attribute its strengths to human editorial choices. The exchange distinguishes accessible AI-assisted production from demonstrated superiority to professional human work.
qs: the former Head of Legal at ASML made all by himself in about a day, using only AI
It's cute as small project but if you judge it by the same standards and demands of a professional film it's crap.
There's no continuity because even if you put in the same prompts every iteration is only the ML tool's best guess.
it is miles ahead of the lame “a day at law firm XYZ” video that your corporate communications team will take days to film and weeks to deliver
The aspects of the film using machine generated footage that make it stand out vs a generic corporate film arise from what appear to be human editorial & creative choices made by its maker.
what he's made belongs to a sub-genre of animation using a new tool rather than a demonstration of ML models superiority to human creatives.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The anonymous participants offer conflicting claims about present AI quality, junior displacement, training, supervision and adoption barriers; the thread does not present a single agreed position.
pts.d: 1. The original poster juxtaposes claims that AI produces poor results and that it produces great results when used properly. Conditional on successful automation of basic tasks, they question how newcomers will learn and predict that only big firms will continue training juniors for succession, potentially seeking commitments of more than five years or repayment of training costs. 2. A participant describing their own large-firm environment reports widespread availability of off-the-shelf and bespoke AI tools, use by younger staff, unchanged partner emphasis on strategy, business development and management, and no observed profitability effect. They suggest, hypothetically rather than as an implemented reduction, that eliminating 50% of expensive juniors would increase partner income. Another participant anticipates harmful graduate underemployment. 3. One participant says machine-learning output inherently contains errors and requires review by people capable of recognising them; another predicts that AI will eventually make fewer errors than severely overworked junior deal lawyers. A further participant compares ChatGPT to a junior lawyer, stressing that it must be supervised accordingly. 4. The response explicitly attributed to MS Copilot—not a view independently advanced by the poster reproducing it—predicts that routine-task automation could shift training toward strategy, negotiation, critical judgment, AI-powered simulations, tool collaboration and deeper mentoring. A subsequent participant rejects the premise that juniors can move straight to strategy, arguing that strategic understanding requires substantive experience. 5. A participant who says they have examined numerous AI tools claims that Copilot's model routing can produce suboptimal answers, that no tool they have examined yet provides dynamic document mark-ups, and that effective prompting matters. They expect the mark-up capability to arrive eventually. 6. Another participant argues that transactional legal AI struggles because firms are disorganised, relevant document volumes are relatively small, and documents are bespoke and poorly connected. They also argue that reluctance to delegate discrete tasks, inadequate supervision and underinvestment in legal technology and information security impede adoption, despite many partial or routine tasks being suitable for AI. 7. A participant describes an allegedly AI-written letter of claim as extremely poor; their assertion that it was generated by AI is an inference, not established provenance. 8. In a secondary discussion of AI-generated film, one participant presents a former ASML legal head's video as evidence of substantial capability outside law; another argues that continuity weaknesses and human creative contributions prevent it from demonstrating superiority over professional human filmmaking. A defender instead claims a speed-and-accessibility advantage over ordinary corporate video production. Comments about oneNDA and oneDPA concern standardisation rather than demonstrated AI effects; wishes to automate privacy work are preferences, not findings.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence offered is chiefly anonymous workplace experience, personal tool use, illustrative reasoning and one linked creative example; the thread supplies no systematic legal-AI performance or employment data.
pts.d: The large-firm participant grounds the adoption and profitability observations in their own workplace, without financial figures, measurement methods or a specified observation period. The 50% junior-reduction figure is a hypothetical cost-saving scenario, not a measured result or announced staffing plan. Predictions about training concentration, retention contracts, graduate employment and future comparative error rates have no supporting study or documented case in the thread. Supervision claims rest on general assertions about machine learning and comparisons with junior lawyers, not measured error rates. The dynamic-mark-up claim is explicitly limited to tools one participant has examined; their account of Copilot routing and Microsoft's economic incentives is asserted without documentation. The transactional-work explanation uses an expressly tentative estimate of approximately 1,000 SPAs annually at top European M&A firms, an analogy involving an inexperienced graduate asked to synthesise bespoke agreements, and personal observations about changing delegation practices. It is not presented as a dataset. The letter-of-claim anecdote supplies neither the letter nor proof of AI authorship. Copilot's proposed training changes are an AI-generated answer, not evidence that these changes are occurring or effective. The film discussion links a video and offers competing qualitative assessments; the claimed one-day production process is reported by a participant rather than independently demonstrated within the thread.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Present-day observations in this 2025 thread are distinct from undated, conditional predictions; no participant supplies a firm timetable for workforce or training transformation.
pts.d: Current claims include younger lawyers' tool use, no observed profitability change, limitations in document mark-up, and organisational obstacles in transactional practices. The opening training concern depends explicitly on AI successfully taking over basic tasks; the predicted five-plus-year contracts refer to the proposed duration of employment commitments, not a forecast date for AI adoption. The partner-income claim depends on actually removing substantial junior staffing costs and does not establish that this is happening. Better performance than exhausted deal lawyers is predicted only 'over time', with that particular human comparator rather than lawyers generally. The supervision requirement is stated as persisting even under ideal circumstances. Copilot's training account is framed as possible adaptation as routine work is automated, and deeper mentoring depends on mentors being freed from basic tasks. The prompting participant qualifies their mark-up assessment with 'so far' and their optimism with 'a matter of time'. The organisational critique makes AI's usefulness dependent on appropriate task decomposition, willingness to accept partial assistance, training and supervision, and investment rather than expecting a perfect complex deliverable. In the film discussion, the assessment turns on the comparison standard: rapid, small-scale or corporate production versus professional filmmaking, and AI-generated material versus the human editorial choices shaping it.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal affected groups are junior lawyers and graduates, large-firm partners, trainers and supervisors, and transactional practices; downstream client effects are largely implicit.
pts.d: Junior lawyers and prospective entrants face the predicted loss of routine learning opportunities, reduced recruitment or staffing, and potentially longer retention commitments or training-cost repayment obligations. The original poster's prediction implies that training opportunities would concentrate in big firms. The graduate-employment response presents exclusion from legal work as a source of severe distress, without supplying labour-market evidence. Partners are portrayed both as continuing their existing strategic, business-development and management roles and as potential beneficiaries of reduced junior payroll. Experienced lawyers retain responsibility for recognising errors and supervising AI-assisted work. In Copilot's proposed adaptation, trainees, law schools, firms and mentors would shift toward simulations, AI literacy, complex reasoning and client-facing skills; the opposing participant says this cannot bypass experiential foundations. The transactional critique particularly concerns bespoke M&A work and European top-tier practices, contrasting it with highly standardised NDA work and discrete support tasks. Legal-technology and information-security functions are identified as underfunded organisational constraints. Clients and recipients of legal documents are implicitly exposed to output-quality problems, illustrated by the allegedly AI-generated letter of claim, but no client-outcome or access-to-justice evidence is offered. The secondary film debate concerns individual creators, corporate communications teams and professional filmmakers, not legal-service delivery.
